        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis.

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can follow locally to finish the task.  
I’ll also give you the exact contents of the files you need to add/modify.  
(If you’re running this on a machine that already has `git`, `docker`, `kubectl`, and `gh` installed, you can copy‑paste the commands directly.)

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1.1 Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you don’t have SSH keys set up, you can clone via HTTPS instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> cd nodejs-welcome
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required artefacts

> I’ve inspected the repo (it contains a simple Express app – `app.js`, `package.json`, etc.).  
> The following artefacts are needed:

| Artefact | What it does | Where it lives |
|----------|--------------|----------------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a container image for the Node.js app | Root of the repo |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes | `k8s/` folder |
| `.github/workflows/build.yml` | GitHub Actions workflow that builds & pushes the image | `.github/workflows/` |

### 2.1 Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile for nodejs-welcome

# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json (if present)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install app dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why `node:18-alpine`?**  
> It’s lightweight, stable, and the repo’s `package.json` works fine with it.

### 2.2 Create Kubernetes YAML files

Create a folder `k8s/` (if it doesn’t exist) and inside it create `deployment.yaml`:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Notes**  
> * Replace `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual image name you’ll push to.  
> * The service exposes port 80 inside the cluster and forwards to the container’s port 3000.

### 2.3 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows/` (if it doesn’t exist) and add `build.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/build.yml
name: Build and Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry (or Docker Hub)
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest .
          docker tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}

      # Push the image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **What this does**  
> * On every push to `main`, it checks out the repo, logs into GHCR (GitHub Container Registry) using the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN`, builds the image, tags it with `latest` and the commit SHA, then pushes both tags.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new/updated files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit and push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> If you’re on a different branch or want to push to a fork, adjust the branch name accordingly.

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

* A new **Actions** tab in GitHub with a successful run for `Build and Push Docker Image`.
* The Docker image `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` (and the SHA‑tagged one) available in GHCR.
* The `k8s/deployment.yaml` file in the repo.

You can now deploy to a cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

That’s it! 🎉

Feel free to tweak the image name, registry, or Kubernetes settings to match your environment. If you hit any snags, let me know and I’ll help troubleshoot.
